claim: Motivation depends on dopamine, but might be modulated by acetylcholine which influences dopamine release in the striatum.
source: Motivation depends on dopamine, but might be modulated by acetylcholine which influences dopamine release in the striatum, and amplifies motivation in animal studies.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on the relationship between acetylcholine and dopamine in the striatum.

claim: Acetylcholine amplifies motivation in animal studies.
source: Motivation depends on dopamine, but might be modulated by acetylcholine which influences dopamine release in the striatum, and amplifies motivation in animal studies.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from animal studies.

claim: Anticholinergic drugs are frequently used in Parkinson's disease.
source: A corresponding effect in humans would be important clinically, since anticholinergic drugs are frequently used in Parkinson's disease, a condition that can also disrupt motivation.
evidence: This is stated as clinical knowledge about treatment practices.

claim: Parkinson's disease can disrupt motivation.
source: A corresponding effect in humans would be important clinically, since anticholinergic drugs are frequently used in Parkinson's disease, a condition that can also disrupt motivation.
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge.

claim: Reward and dopamine make us more ready to respond, as indexed by reaction times (RT).
source: Reward and dopamine make us more ready to respond, as indexed by reaction times (RT), and move faster, sometimes termed vigour.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the effects of reward and dopamine.

claim: Reward and dopamine make us move faster, sometimes termed vigour.
source: Reward and dopamine make us more ready to respond, as indexed by reaction times (RT), and move faster, sometimes termed vigour.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the effects of reward and dopamine.

claim: Preparatory processes that control reaction time and vigour can be tracked using electroencephalography (EEG).
source: These effects may be controlled by preparatory processes that can be tracked using electroencephalography (EEG).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological premise for the study.

claim: Participants responded faster when incentives were high.
source: Participants responded faster and with greater vigour when incentives were high, but THP blunted these motivational effects, suggesting that muscarinic receptors facilitate invigoration by reward.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Participants responded with greater vigour when incentives were high.
source: Participants responded faster and with greater vigour when incentives were high, but THP blunted these motivational effects, suggesting that muscarinic receptors facilitate invigoration by reward.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: THP blunted the motivational effects of high incentives on response speed and vigour.
source: Participants responded faster and with greater vigour when incentives were high, but THP blunted these motivational effects, suggesting that muscarinic receptors facilitate invigoration by reward.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Muscarinic receptors facilitate invigoration by reward.
source: Participants responded faster and with greater vigour when incentives were high, but THP blunted these motivational effects, suggesting that muscarinic receptors facilitate invigoration by reward.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Preparatory EEG build-up (contingent negative variation [CNV]) was strengthened by high incentives.
source: Preparatory EEG build-up (contingent negative variation [CNV]) was strengthened by high incentives and by muscarinic blockade, although THP reduced the incentive effect.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the EEG data.

claim: Preparatory EEG build-up (contingent negative variation [CNV]) was strengthened by muscarinic blockade.
source: Preparatory EEG build-up (contingent negative variation [CNV]) was strengthened by high incentives and by muscarinic blockade, although THP reduced the incentive effect.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the EEG data.

claim: THP reduced the incentive effect on CNV.
source: Preparatory EEG build-up (contingent negative variation [CNV]) was strengthened by high incentives and by muscarinic blockade, although THP reduced the incentive effect.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the EEG data.

claim: The amplitude of preparatory activity predicted both vigour and RT, although over distinct scalp regions.
source: The amplitude of preparatory activity predicted both vigour and RT, although over distinct scalp regions; frontal activity predicted vigour, whereas a larger, earlier, central component predicted RT.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the EEG analysis.

claim: Frontal activity predicted vigour.
source: The amplitude of preparatory activity predicted both vigour and RT, although over distinct scalp regions; frontal activity predicted vigour, whereas a larger, earlier, central component predicted RT.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the EEG analysis.

claim: A larger, earlier, central component predicted RT.
source: The amplitude of preparatory activity predicted both vigour and RT, although over distinct scalp regions; frontal activity predicted vigour, whereas a larger, earlier, central component predicted RT.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the EEG analysis.

claim: The incentivisation of RT was partly mediated by the CNV.
source: The incentivisation of RT was partly mediated by the CNV, though vigour was not.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the mediation analysis.

claim: The incentivisation of vigour was not mediated by the CNV.
source: The incentivisation of RT was partly mediated by the CNV, though vigour was not.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the mediation analysis.

claim: The CNV mediated the drug's effect on dampening incentives.
source: Moreover, the CNV mediated the drug's effect on dampening incentives, suggesting that muscarinic receptors underlie the motivational influence on this preparatory activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the mediated moderation analysis.

claim: Muscarinic receptors underlie the motivational influence on preparatory activity.
source: Moreover, the CNV mediated the drug's effect on dampening incentives, suggesting that muscarinic receptors underlie the motivational influence on this preparatory activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mediation findings.

claim: A muscarinic blocker impairs motivated action in healthy people.
source: Taken together, these findings show that a muscarinic blocker impairs motivated action in healthy people, and that medial frontal preparatory neural activity mediates this for RT.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental findings.

claim: Medial frontal preparatory neural activity mediates the effect of muscarinic blockade on RT.
source: Taken together, these findings show that a muscarinic blocker impairs motivated action in healthy people, and that medial frontal preparatory neural activity mediates this for RT.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental findings.

claim: Motivation is our ability to exert effort to obtain reward.
source: Motivation is our ability to exert effort to obtain reward, and can be dramatically impacted in psychiatric and neurological disorders.
evidence: This is a definitional statement.

claim: Motivation can be dramatically impacted in psychiatric and neurological disorders.
source: Motivation is our ability to exert effort to obtain reward, and can be dramatically impacted in psychiatric and neurological disorders.
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge.

claim: Response vigour is an increase in movement speed with reward.
source: One simple index of motivation is response vigour: an increase in movement speed with reward (Dudman and Krakauer, 2016; Shadmehr et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citations.

claim: Motivation and the lack of motivation (apathy) have been linked to dopamine.
source: Motivation and the lack of motivation (apathy) have been linked to dopamine (McGuigan et al., 2019; Walton and Bouret, 2019), and accordingly, vigour is reduced in Parkinson's disease (Beierholm et al., 2013; da Silva et al., 2018; Mazzoni et al., 2007; Zénon et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Vigour is reduced in Parkinson's disease.
source: Motivation and the lack of motivation (apathy) have been linked to dopamine (McGuigan et al., 2019; Walton and Bouret, 2019), and accordingly, vigour is reduced in Parkinson's disease (Beierholm et al., 2013; da Silva et al., 2018; Mazzoni et al., 2007; Zénon et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Striatal dopamine levels ramp up before potentially rewarding actions.
source: Striatal dopamine levels ramp up before potentially rewarding actions.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from animal work.

claim: Acetylcholine controls dopaminergic effects via both firing rates and local release in the striatum.
source: Animal work demonstrates that acetylcholine controls these dopaminergic effects, via both firing rates (Forster and Blaha, 2000; Mark et al., 2011) and local release in the striatum (Cachope and Cheer, 2014; Shen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from animal work, supported by citations.

claim: Acetylcholine provides two mechanisms to affect motivation.
source: These provide two mechanisms for acetylcholine to affect motivation (Collins et al., 2019; Hoebel et al., 2007), with muscarinic receptors in nucleus accumbens playing an important role in facilitating reward-related vigour (Collins et al., 2016), possibly by potentiating dopamine release and affecting the frequency sensitivity of striatal dopaminergic terminals (Collins et al., 2016; Threlfell et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Muscarinic receptors in nucleus accumbens play an important role in facilitating reward-related vigour.
source: These provide two mechanisms for acetylcholine to affect motivation (Collins et al., 2019; Hoebel et al., 2007), with muscarinic receptors in nucleus accumbens playing an important role in facilitating reward-related vigour (Collins et al., 2016), possibly by potentiating dopamine release and affecting the frequency sensitivity of striatal dopaminergic terminals (Collins et al., 2016; Threlfell et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Muscarinic receptors in nucleus accumbens possibly facilitate reward-related vigour by potentiating dopamine release and affecting the frequency sensitivity of striatal dopaminergic terminals.
source: These provide two mechanisms for acetylcholine to affect motivation (Collins et al., 2019; Hoebel et al., 2007), with muscarinic receptors in nucleus accumbens playing an important role in facilitating reward-related vigour (Collins et al., 2016), possibly by potentiating dopamine release and affecting the frequency sensitivity of striatal dopaminergic terminals (Collins et al., 2016; Threlfell et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a speculative mechanism supported by citations.

claim: The ultimate effect of systemic muscarinic drugs on motivation is complex.
source: However, the ultimate effect of systemic muscarinic drugs on motivation is complex.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of conflicting findings in the literature.

claim: Muscarinic antagonism has impaired motivation in some animal studies.
source: Muscarinic antagonism has impaired motivation in some animal studies (Collins et al., 2016; Ostlund et al., 2014; Pratt and Kelley, 2004), while improving it in others (Hailwood et al., 2019; Nunes et al., 2013), and even less is known of how they affect humans.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Muscarinic antagonism has improved motivation in some animal studies.
source: Muscarinic antagonism has impaired motivation in some animal studies (Collins et al., 2016; Ostlund et al., 2014; Pratt and Kelley, 2004), while improving it in others (Hailwood et al., 2019; Nunes et al., 2013), and even less is known of how they affect humans.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Even less is known of how muscarinic drugs affect motivation in humans.
source: Muscarinic antagonism has impaired motivation in some animal studies (Collins et al., 2016; Ostlund et al., 2014; Pratt and Kelley, 2004), while improving it in others (Hailwood et al., 2019; Nunes et al., 2013), and even less is known of how they affect humans.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap.

claim: Pro-cholinergic drugs may ameliorate clinical apathy.
source: Pro-cholinergic drugs may ameliorate clinical apathy, a disabling symptom seen in around 50% of patients with Parkinson's disease (Devos et al., 2014; Fahed and Steffens, 2021; Pagonabarraga et al., 2015), yet cholinergic blockers are commonly used to treat the motor symptoms.
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Apathy is a disabling symptom seen in around 50% of patients with Parkinson's disease.
source: Pro-cholinergic drugs may ameliorate clinical apathy, a disabling symptom seen in around 50% of patients with Parkinson's disease (Devos et al., 2014; Fahed and Steffens, 2021; Pagonabarraga et al., 2015), yet cholinergic blockers are commonly used to treat the motor symptoms.
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cholinergic blockers are commonly used to treat the motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease.
source: Pro-cholinergic drugs may ameliorate clinical apathy, a disabling symptom seen in around 50% of patients with Parkinson's disease (Devos et al., 2014; Fahed and Steffens, 2021; Pagonabarraga et al., 2015), yet cholinergic blockers are commonly used to treat the motor symptoms.
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge.

claim: Clinicians face a dilemma when treating patients with both tremor and apathy/cognitive impairment.
source: This frequently puts clinicians in a dilemma when treating patients with both tremor, which responds well to anticholinergic drugs such as trihexyphenidyl (THP), but also apathy and cognitive impairment, which both respond to pro-cholinergic drugs (Bohnen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated as a clinical challenge supported by citations.

claim: Tremor responds well to anticholinergic drugs such as trihexyphenidyl (THP).
source: This frequently puts clinicians in a dilemma when treating patients with both tremor, which responds well to anticholinergic drugs such as trihexyphenidyl (THP), but also apathy and cognitive impairment, which both respond to pro-cholinergic drugs (Bohnen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Apathy and cognitive impairment both respond to pro-cholinergic drugs.
source: This frequently puts clinicians in a dilemma when treating patients with both tremor, which responds well to anticholinergic drugs such as trihexyphenidyl (THP), but also apathy and cognitive impairment, which both respond to pro-cholinergic drugs (Bohnen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Distinguishing the mechanisms by which acetylcholine receptors contribute to movement and motivation will be critical for selecting appropriate treatments in patients with Parkinson's disease.
source: Distinguishing the mechanisms by which acetylcholine receptors contribute to movement and motivation will be critical for selecting appropriate treatments in these patients.
evidence: This is stated as a clinical rationale for the research.

claim: Motivation influences action selection and movement invigoration based on the motivational state that is set up before the action.
source: Motivation influences action selection and movement invigoration based on the motivational state that is set up before the action.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical premise.

claim: One potential mechanism of motivation may be preparatory activation of frontal premotor areas.
source: One potential mechanism of this may be preparatory activation of frontal premotor areas, which may be indexed on electroencephalography (EEG) by the contingent negative variation (CNV; Walter et al., 1964), a slow negative potential that appears between a warning stimulus and a prompt to act (Brunia et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: The contingent negative variation (CNV) is a slow negative potential that appears between a warning stimulus and a prompt to act.
source: One potential mechanism of this may be preparatory activation of frontal premotor areas, which may be indexed on electroencephalography (EEG) by the contingent negative variation (CNV; Walter et al., 1964), a slow negative potential that appears between a warning stimulus and a prompt to act (Brunia et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citations.

claim: Early models of the CNV proposed that it reflected cholinergic activity, modulated by dopamine, noradrenaline, and GABA.
source: Early models of the CNV proposed that it reflected cholinergic activity, modulated by dopamine, noradrenaline, and GABA (Timsit-Berthier, 1991).
evidence: This is stated as historical knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Muscarinic antagonists were found to disrupt the CNV in rodents.
source: Supporting this, muscarinic antagonists were found to disrupt the CNV in rodents (Ebenezer, 1986; Papart et al., 1997; Pirch et al., 1986; Papart et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from animal studies, supported by citations.

claim: The CNV reflects preparatory activation of supplementary motor area and anterior cingulate, that can be amplified by reward signals from ventral striatum.
source: This anticipatory signal reflects preparatory activation of supplementary motor area and anterior cingulate, that can be amplified by reward signals from ventral striatum (Nagai et al., 2004; Plichta et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The CNV is decreased by depression.
source: As a marker of motivation, the CNV is of great clinical interest, being decreased by depression (Ansseau et al., 1985) and Parkinson's disease (Ikeda et al., 1997), and conversely, increased by dopaminergic medications (Linssen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The CNV is decreased by Parkinson's disease.
source: As a marker of motivation, the CNV is of great clinical interest, being decreased by depression (Ansseau et al., 1985) and Parkinson's disease (Ikeda et al., 1997), and conversely, increased by dopaminergic medications (Linssen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The CNV is increased by dopaminergic medications.
source: As a marker of motivation, the CNV is of great clinical interest, being decreased by depression (Ansseau et al., 1985) and Parkinson's disease (Ikeda et al., 1997), and conversely, increased by dopaminergic medications (Linssen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The CNV is strengthened by monetary incentives dependent on performance.
source: Accordingly, the CNV is strengthened by monetary incentives dependent on performance (Berchio et al., 2019; Novak et al., 2016; Novak and Foti, 2015) and reward contingency (Frömer et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The CNV is strengthened by reward contingency.
source: Accordingly, the CNV is strengthened by monetary incentives dependent on performance (Berchio et al., 2019; Novak et al., 2016; Novak and Foti, 2015) and reward contingency (Frömer et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Changes in the CNV could provide a mechanistic handle on the effect of drugs on motivation.
source: Changes in the CNV could therefore provide a mechanistic handle on the effect of drugs on motivation.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical rationale for the study.

claim: Residual peak velocity was increased by incentives (β=0.1266, p<0.0001).
source: As predicted, residual peak velocity was increased by incentives (Figure 1d; β=0.1266, p<0.0001), while distractors slightly slowed residual velocity (β=–0.0158, p=0.0294; see Table 1 for full behavioural statistics).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Distractors slightly slowed residual velocity (β=–0.0158, p=0.0294).
source: As predicted, residual peak velocity was increased by incentives (Figure 1d; β=0.1266, p<0.0001), while distractors slightly slowed residual velocity (β=–0.0158, p=0.0294; see Table 1 for full behavioural statistics).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: THP decreased the effect of incentives on velocity (incentive * THP: β=–0.0216, p=0.0030).
source: THP decreased the effect of incentives on velocity (incentive * THP: β=–0.0216, p=0.0030), indicating that muscarinic blockade diminished motivation by incentives.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Muscarinic blockade diminished motivation by incentives.
source: THP decreased the effect of incentives on velocity (incentive * THP: β=–0.0216, p=0.0030), indicating that muscarinic blockade diminished motivation by incentives.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical findings.

claim: High incentives decreased RT (β=–0.0767, p<0.0001).
source: Saccadic RT (time to initiation of saccade) was slower when participants were given THP (β=0.0244, p=<0.0001), faster with incentives (Figure 1e; β=–0.0767, p<0.0001), and slowed by distractors (β=0.0358, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Saccadic RT was slower when participants were given THP (β=0.0244, p=<0.0001).
source: Saccadic RT (time to initiation of saccade) was slower when participants were given THP (β=0.0244, p=<0.0001), faster with incentives (Figure 1e; β=–0.0767, p<0.0001), and slowed by distractors (β=0.0358, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Saccadic RT was slowed by distractors (β=0.0358, p<0.0001).
source: Saccadic RT (time to initiation of saccade) was slower when participants were given THP (β=0.0244, p=<0.0001), faster with incentives (Figure 1e; β=–0.0767, p<0.0001), and slowed by distractors (β=0.0358, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: THP reduced the effects of incentives on RT (incentive*THP: β=0.0218, p=0.0002).
source: Again, THP reduced the effects of incentives (incentive*THP: β=0.0218, p=0.0002).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: When the distractor did not light up, the mean distractor angle was negative (i.e. away from the distractor angle), indicating repulsion away from the angle of the distractor.
source: When the distractor did not light up, the mean distractor angle was negative (i.e. away from the distractor angle), indicating repulsion away from the angle of the distractor, whereas when the distractor lit up and was salient the mean angle was biased towards the distractor (Figure 2b; β=0.2446, p<0.0001; see Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: When the distractor lit up and was salient the mean angle was biased towards the distractor (β=0.2446, p<0.0001).
source: When the distractor did not light up, the mean distractor angle was negative (i.e. away from the distractor angle), indicating repulsion away from the angle of the distractor, whereas when the distractor lit up and was salient the mean angle was biased towards the distractor (Figure 2b; β=0.2446, p<0.0001; see Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: THP increased the pull (main effect of drug, β=0.0283, p<0.0001), but only when the distractor was salient (THP*distractor, β=0.0226, p=0.0012).
source: Single-trial linear mixed-effects regression found that THP increased the pull (main effect of drug, β=0.0283, p<0.0001), but only when the distractor was salient (THP*distractor, β=0.0226, p=0.0012, pairwise drug effect: distractor absent: p>0.3; present: β=0.0511, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: No effect of incentives on distraction was found (β=0.0023, p=0.7444).
source: Unlike in previous work, we found no effect of incentives on distraction (β=0.0023, p=0.7444), although speed-accuracy trade-off curves (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) showed that incentives sped up responses in such a way that distraction was reduced for a given RT.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Speed-accuracy trade-off curves showed that incentives sped up responses in such a way that distraction was reduced for a given RT.
source: Unlike in previous work, we found no effect of incentives on distraction (β=0.0023, p=0.7444), although speed-accuracy trade-off curves (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) showed that incentives sped up responses in such a way that distraction was reduced for a given RT.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of speed-accuracy trade-off curves shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: THP reduced the probability of repulsion around –30°, indicating that THP reduced the repulsion away from the distractor's location.
source: THP reduced the probability of repulsion (Figure 2d) around –30°, indicating that THP reduced the repulsion away from the distractor's location.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of distractor pull distributions shown in Figure 2d.

claim: THP reduced repulsion suggests weaker attentional suppression of the distractor.
source: This suggests weaker attentional suppression of the distractor.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the distractor pull findings.

claim: Incentives had little effect on the distribution of distractor pull.
source: Incentives had little effect on the distribution (yellow line) in keeping with the averages in Figure 2b.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of distractor pull distributions shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Acetylcholine antagonism reduced the invigoration of saccades by incentives.
source: Therefore, acetylcholine antagonism reduced the invigoration of saccades by incentives, and decreased the repulsion of salient distractors.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the behavioral findings.

claim: Acetylcholine antagonism decreased the repulsion of salient distractors.
source: Therefore, acetylcholine antagonism reduced the invigoration of saccades by incentives, and decreased the repulsion of salient distractors.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the behavioral findings.

claim: There was an early fronto-central positive event-related potential (ERP) with a peak around 220 ms, consistent with the P3a.
source: There was an early fronto-central positive event-related potential (ERP) with a peak around 220 ms, consistent with the P3a (Figure 3a), which was then followed by a growing negative potential centrally, consistent with the CNV.
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The early ERP was followed by a growing negative potential centrally, consistent with the CNV.
source: There was an early fronto-central positive event-related potential (ERP) with a peak around 220 ms, consistent with the P3a (Figure 3a), which was then followed by a growing negative potential centrally, consistent with the CNV.
evidence: This is a finding from the EEG analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: THP strengthened negativity in the late ERP to the incentive cue (β=–0.0597, p<0.0001).
source: Prior to the preparation cue (900–1100 ms after incentive cue, baselining at the incentive cue; green shaded area in Figure 3a), THP strengthened negativity (Figure 3b, β=–0.0597, p<0.0001; see Table 2 for full ERP statistics), but incentives had no effect or interaction (p>0.05).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the statistical analysis of EEG data.

claim: Incentives had no effect or interaction on the late ERP to the incentive cue (p>0.05).
source: Prior to the preparation cue (900–1100 ms after incentive cue, baselining at the incentive cue; green shaded area in Figure 3a), THP strengthened negativity (Figure 3b, β=–0.0597, p<0.0001; see Table 2 for full ERP statistics), but incentives had no effect or interaction (p>0.05).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the statistical analysis of EEG data.

claim: The P3a was significantly smaller for high incentive trials (β=–0.0187, p=0.0142) with no other significant effects (p>0.1).
source: After the preparation cue, the P3a (Figure 3c) was significantly smaller for high incentive trials (β=–0.0187, p=0.0142) with no other significant effects (p>0.1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the statistical analysis of EEG data.

claim: The CNV was strengthened (i.e. more negative) by incentive (β=–0.0928, p<0.0001).
source: The subsequent CNV was strengthened (i.e. more negative; Figure 3d) by incentive (β=–0.0928, p<0.0001) and THP (β=–0.0502, p<0.0001), with an interaction whereby THP decreased the incentive effect (β=0.0172, p=0.0213).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the statistical analysis of EEG data.

claim: The CNV was strengthened by THP (β=–0.0502, p<0.0001).
source: The subsequent CNV was strengthened (i.e. more negative; Figure 3d) by incentive (β=–0.0928, p<0.0001) and THP (β=–0.0502, p<0.0001), with an interaction whereby THP decreased the incentive effect (β=0.0172, p=0.0213).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the statistical analysis of EEG data.

claim: There was an interaction whereby THP decreased the incentive effect on CNV (β=0.0172, p=0.0213).
source: The subsequent CNV was strengthened (i.e. more negative; Figure 3d) by incentive (β=–0.0928, p<0.0001) and THP (β=–0.0502, p<0.0001), with an interaction whereby THP decreased the incentive effect (β=0.0172, p=0.0213).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the statistical analysis of EEG data.

claim: The incentive effect on CNV grows more slowly in the THP condition than the placebo condition.
source: Figure 3i shows the incentive effect grows more slowly in the THP condition than the placebo condition.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of difference waves shown in Figure 3i.

claim: Incentives strengthened the CNV, replicating previous work.
source: The CNV in the lead up to the target appearing was strengthened by the incentives, replicating previous work (Frömer et al., 2021; Novak et al., 2016; Novak and Foti, 2015; Schevernels et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding that replicates prior research, supported by citations.

claim: M1r antagonism reduced the effect of incentives on CNV, mirroring the reduced incentivisation on RT and residual velocity.
source: M1r antagonism reduced the effect of incentives on CNV, mirroring the reduced incentivisation on RT and residual velocity.
evidence: This is a summary of the parallel findings in EEG and behavior.

claim: Cholinergic transmission is needed at an early stage of motivational preparation.
source: This suggests that cholinergic transmission is needed at an early stage of motivational preparation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the CNV findings.

claim: CNV amplitude predicted RT, along with distractor pull.
source: CNV amplitude predicted RT, along with distractor pull, and frontal activity in this same time-window predicted residual velocity, aligning with recent studies linking CNV to RT and accuracy (Frömer et al., 2021), and to incentivisation of effort (Berchio et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the regression analysis.

claim: Frontal activity in the CNV time-window predicted residual velocity.
source: CNV amplitude predicted RT, along with distractor pull, and frontal activity in this same time-window predicted residual velocity, aligning with recent studies linking CNV to RT and accuracy (Frömer et al., 2021), and to incentivisation of effort (Berchio et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the regression analysis.

claim: The associations between CNV and behavior held up even when controlling for the other behavioural variables.
source: Our associations held up even when controlling for the other behavioural variables, suggesting they were not due to factors such as the negative correlation of RT and velocity.
evidence: This is a finding from the control analysis.

claim: Incentives determine a baseline level of motivation, dependent on acetylcholine, that is integrated while we decide to act, thus influencing the speed of action initiation.
source: Together these findings suggest that incentives determine a baseline level of motivation, dependent on acetylcholine, that is integrated while we decide to act, thus influencing the speed of action initiation.
